BEIJING, China (CNN) -- Chinese officials in the northwestern Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region reported the death of a fourth baby Thursday in the country's expanding contaminated infant formula case. The tainted milk powder has already sickened more than 6,200 babies. Earlier in the day, authorities announced the arrest of 12 more suspects in the investigation, provincial police said. The arrests bring to 18 the number of people detained, according to the Hebei Public Security Bureau. Twelve of those arrested are involved in the collection of milk and the production of milk products, authorities said. Authorities accuse the other six of illegally selling the chemical added to the milk. More than 1,300 infants are hospitalized, said Li Changjiang, China's director of quarantine and inspection, on Wednesday. Their conditions include malnutrition, kidney stones and acute renal failure. Inspectors have been deployed across the country to test producers' inventories. Of China's 175 baby milk powder production companies, 66 have stopped production, Li said. Watch parents scramble for safe milk » . Two brothers who sold fresh milk used to produce contaminated baby milk powder were arrested by Chinese investigators Monday. They could face death if convicted, according to China Daily, a state-run newspaper. The raw milk had been watered down and a chemical added to fool quality checks, the newspaper said. Investigators said the brothers confessed to watering down the raw milk and mixing in tripolycyanamide, also known as melamine. They said they did it to recover losses suffered when the factory rejected earlier milk shipments, the paper reported.  Learn more about the chemical melamine » . The brothers are charged with producing and selling toxic and hazardous food, which carries a possible death penalty, the paper said. Health experts say ingesting melamine can lead to kidney stones, urinary tract ulcers, and eye and skin irritation. The chemical is commonly used in coatings and laminates, wood adhesives, fabric coatings, ceiling tiles and flame retardants.  Watch CNN visit the company at the center of the scandal » . Thousands of tons of the tainted milk powder have been recalled, including pullbacks by Mengniu Dairy Group, China's largest milk producer, and the Sanlu Group. Chinese investigators have found melamine in nearly 70 milk products from more than 20 companies, Li said Wednesday. Products made by Sanlu had the highest concentration of the chemical. It is not the first time Sanlu has been connected to a scandal involving tainted milk powder, according to China Daily. In 2004, at least 13 infants in the eastern Anhui province died of malnutrition after drinking milk powder that had little to no nutrition. The illegally manufactured milk was falsely labeled with the Sanlu brand, according to the paper. The vast majority of the tainted formula was consumed domestically, but it is known to have been exported to Taiwan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Yemen, Chad and Burundi, according to Li. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration said no Chinese baby formula has been allowed on the market in the United States. In a statement on its Web site, the FDA said it had reached out to all five companies making formula in the United States and none has used formula or source materials from China. This episode marks the latest in a string of tainted products produced in China: . CNN's Yuli Yang contributed to this story.

**BEIJING, China (CNN) —** Chinese officials in the northwestern Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region reported the death of a fourth baby Thursday as the country’s contaminated infant formula crisis continued to expand. The tainted milk powder has already sickened more than 6,200 babies.

Earlier Thursday, authorities announced the arrest of 12 additional suspects in the investigation, provincial police said. The arrests bring the total number of people detained to 18, according to the Hebei Public Security Bureau.

Authorities said 12 of those arrested were involved in collecting milk and producing milk products. The other six are accused of illegally selling the chemical added to the milk.

More than 1,300 infants are hospitalized with conditions including malnutrition, kidney stones and acute renal failure, Li Changjiang, China’s director of quarantine and inspection, said Wednesday.

Inspectors have been deployed nationwide to test producers’ inventories. Of China’s 175 baby milk powder production companies, 66 have halted production, Li said.

*Watch parents scramble for safe milk »*

Chinese investigators arrested two brothers Monday who sold fresh milk used to make contaminated baby milk powder. If convicted, they could face the death penalty, according to the state-run newspaper *China Daily*.

The raw milk had been diluted with water, and a chemical was added to deceive quality-control tests, the newspaper reported. Investigators said the brothers confessed to watering down the raw milk and mixing in tripolycyanamide, also known as melamine. They said they did so to recover losses incurred when the factory rejected earlier milk shipments, according to the paper.

*Learn more about the chemical melamine »*

The brothers have been charged with producing and selling toxic and hazardous food, an offense that carries a possible death sentence, the paper said.

Health experts say ingesting melamine can cause kidney stones, urinary tract ulcers, and eye and skin irritation. The chemical is commonly used in coatings and laminates, wood adhesives, fabric coatings, ceiling tiles and flame retardants.

*Watch CNN visit the company at the center of the scandal »*

Thousands of tons of tainted milk powder have been recalled, including products withdrawn by Mengniu Dairy Group, China’s largest milk producer, and the Sanlu Group.

Chinese investigators have detected melamine in nearly 70 milk products made by more than 20 companies, Li said Wednesday. Products manufactured by Sanlu contained the highest concentration of the chemical.

This is not the first time Sanlu has been linked to a tainted milk powder scandal, according to *China Daily*. In 2004, at least 13 infants in the eastern province of Anhui died of malnutrition after consuming milk powder that had little or no nutritional value. The illegally manufactured milk was falsely labeled with the Sanlu brand, the newspaper reported.

The vast majority of the tainted formula was consumed domestically, but it is known to have been exported to Taiwan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Yemen, Chad and Burundi, according to Li.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration said no Chinese baby formula has been permitted for sale in the United States. In a statement posted on its website, the FDA said it had contacted all five companies that manufacture formula in the United States, and none had used formula or source materials from China.

The episode is the latest in a series of cases involving tainted products made in China.

CNN’s Yuli Yang contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
BEIJING, China (CNN) — The widening scandal over contaminated baby formula in China claimed a fourth infant’s life on Thursday, officials in the northwestern Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region said. More than 6,200 babies have become ill after consuming the adulterated milk powder.

Earlier Thursday, provincial police reported that investigators had taken another 12 suspects into custody. According to the Hebei Public Security Bureau, the latest arrests raised the total number of detainees to 18. Officials said 12 were connected to milk collection and dairy-product manufacturing, while the remaining six were accused of unlawfully selling the chemical mixed into the milk.

Li Changjiang, China’s head of quarantine and inspection, said Wednesday that over 1,300 infants remained in hospitals. Their medical problems included malnutrition, kidney stones and acute kidney failure.

Inspection teams have been sent throughout China to examine dairy producers’ stock. Li said 66 of the country’s 175 infant milk-powder manufacturers had halted operations. Parents, meanwhile, were rushing to find formula considered safe.

On Monday, Chinese investigators arrested two brothers who had supplied fresh milk later used to manufacture the contaminated formula. If found guilty, they could be sentenced to death, the state-run China Daily reported.

According to the newspaper, the raw milk was diluted with water, then treated with a chemical intended to deceive quality-control tests. Investigators said the brothers admitted adding tripolycyanamide—also called melamine—after watering down the milk. They reportedly said they were trying to recoup money lost when a factory rejected previous deliveries.

The men were charged with making and distributing poisonous and dangerous food, an offense that can carry the death penalty, China Daily said.

Medical specialists say consuming melamine may cause kidney stones, ulcers in the urinary tract, and irritation of the eyes and skin. The substance is ordinarily used in products such as laminates and coatings, adhesives for wood, fabric finishes, ceiling tiles and flame-retardant materials.

Recalls have covered thousands of tons of contaminated milk powder. Among the companies withdrawing products were Sanlu Group and Mengniu Dairy Group, China’s biggest milk producer.

Li said Wednesday that investigators had detected melamine in almost 70 dairy products made by more than 20 businesses. Sanlu products contained the greatest levels of the chemical. CNN also visited the company at the center of the controversy.

China Daily reported that Sanlu’s name had previously surfaced in a tainted-formula case. In 2004, at least 13 babies in eastern China’s Anhui province died from malnutrition after being fed milk powder with little or no nutritional content. The newspaper said the illegally produced formula had falsely carried Sanlu branding.

Although most of the contaminated formula was consumed within China, Li said exports were known to have reached Taiwan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Yemen, Chad and Burundi.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration said infant formula manufactured in China had not been permitted for sale in the United States. In a statement posted online, the agency said it had contacted all five U.S. formula producers, and each confirmed that it had used neither Chinese formula nor ingredients sourced from China.

The case was the latest in a series involving contaminated goods made in China.

CNN’s Yuli Yang contributed to the report.

Chinese authorities have launched a broad investigation into a growing infant-formula contamination scandal, arresting suspects, inspecting dairy producers and ordering dozens of companies to suspend production. Investigators say raw milk was diluted and then adulterated with melamine, an industrial chemical that can make watered-down milk appear to contain more protein during routine quality tests.

The contaminated formula has killed four babies and sickened more than 6,200 children. More than 1,300 infants have been hospitalized, some suffering from kidney stones, acute renal failure and other serious urinary complications. Hospitals have been instructed to screen children who consumed the affected products and provide emergency treatment where necessary.

Testing has found melamine in products from numerous dairy companies, widening the crisis beyond the manufacturer first linked to the illnesses. Authorities are examining producers’ inventories, recalling contaminated formula and stopping production at plants that failed safety checks. Investigators are also tracing the milk-collection network to determine where the chemical was added and whether company officials knew that contaminated ingredients were entering the supply chain.

Melamine is used in the manufacture of plastics, adhesives and other industrial products and is not approved for use in food. Because standard tests estimate protein content by measuring nitrogen, adding the nitrogen-rich chemical can disguise the low protein level of milk that has been diluted with water. In infants, exposure can cause crystals to form in the kidneys, potentially leading to stones, blockages and kidney failure.

The scandal has exposed serious weaknesses in China’s food-safety system, including poor oversight of milk suppliers, inadequate testing and delays in alerting the public. Officials have promised a nationwide review of the dairy industry and stricter monitoring from farms and collection stations to processing plants and retailers.

Suspects accused of producing or selling adulterated milk face severe criminal charges. Authorities have said that anyone found to have knowingly endangered consumers, concealed evidence or obstructed the investigation will be prosecuted. The government is also under pressure to explain how contaminated formula remained on the market long enough to harm thousands of children and to ensure that families receive medical care and compensation.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a detailed CNN-style article on the Chinese infant formula contamination scandal, covering the death toll, suspects arrested, health effects of melamine, implicated dairy companies, exports, and the FDA response.
counterfactuals.output:
# China’s melamine-tainted milk scandal killed six infants and sickened hundreds of thousands

**BEIJING —** One of China’s worst food-safety crises began with an attempt to conceal watered-down milk and ended with six infants dead, hundreds of thousands of children affected and a global recall of Chinese-made dairy products.

In 2008, investigators found that suppliers had added **melamine**, an industrial chemical rich in nitrogen, to raw milk. The substance could make diluted milk appear to contain more protein when tested using methods that estimated protein levels by measuring nitrogen.

The contamination spread through China’s dairy supply chain and into infant formula, milk powder, candy, cookies, coffee drinks and other foods. The scandal implicated some of the country’s largest dairy companies, triggered criminal prosecutions and exposed serious weaknesses in food regulation and corporate oversight.

## Six deaths and hundreds of thousands of cases

Chinese authorities ultimately attributed **at least six infant deaths** to the contamination. About **300,000 children were reported to have been affected**, with tens of thousands receiving hospital treatment. Official figures said more than 50,000 children were hospitalized at various points during the crisis.

Many of the victims were babies who depended heavily or exclusively on formula. Parents reported symptoms including painful urination, blood in the urine, vomiting and unexplained crying.

The full scale of the outbreak emerged only after doctors identified unusual numbers of kidney stones in very young children — a condition considered rare among infants.

## How melamine damaged children’s kidneys

Melamine is used in products such as plastics, laminates, adhesives and flame-resistant materials. It is not approved as an ingredient in food.

Although melamine by itself has relatively low acute toxicity, consuming it in significant amounts can cause crystals to form in the urinary system. The danger can increase when melamine combines with related chemicals, including cyanuric acid, producing insoluble crystals.

In infants, exposure was linked to:

- Kidney stones  
- Urinary tract blockages  
- Blood in the urine  
- Reduced urine production  
- Kidney inflammation  
- Acute kidney failure  
- Death in the most severe cases  

Infants were especially vulnerable because of their small body size, developing kidneys and reliance on formula as a primary source of nutrition.

## Sanlu at the center of the crisis

The company most closely associated with the scandal was **Sanlu Group**, then one of China’s biggest producers of infant formula. Tests found extremely high melamine concentrations in some Sanlu products.

Sanlu recalled hundreds of tons of formula in September 2008. The company later collapsed and was declared bankrupt.

Investigations showed that complaints and indications of a problem had surfaced before the scandal became public. Sanlu was criticized for failing to act quickly enough and for delaying disclosure while the 2008 Beijing Olympics were underway.

Fonterra, a New Zealand dairy cooperative that owned a major stake in Sanlu, said it had pushed for a recall after learning of the contamination. New Zealand officials later said they intervened after becoming concerned that local action was too slow.

## Major dairy brands implicated

Sanlu was not the only producer affected. Chinese inspectors tested products from more than 100 companies and reported finding melamine in infant formula made by **22 dairy companies**.

Among the major brands whose products tested positive were:

- **Sanlu Group**  
- **China Mengniu Dairy**  
- **Inner Mongolia Yili Industrial Group**  
- **Bright Dairy & Food**  

The levels varied widely among products and companies. Sanlu’s formula contained some of the highest concentrations, while lower levels were detected in products from other manufacturers.

The discoveries damaged public confidence across China’s dairy sector. Supermarkets removed products, families sought imported formula, and governments ordered mass screening of infants.

## Suppliers and company officials arrested

Chinese police arrested and detained numerous suspects, including milk collectors, dairy suppliers and people accused of manufacturing or selling melamine mixtures.

Early in the investigation, authorities in Hebei province — where Sanlu was based — reported detaining **at least 18 suspects**, including people accused of adding melamine to raw milk or selling the chemical to suppliers. The number increased as the investigation widened.

Prosecutors later brought criminal cases against **21 defendants** connected to the scandal.

Among the most prominent was **Tian Wenhua**, Sanlu’s former chairwoman and general manager. She was convicted of producing and selling fake or substandard products and received a life sentence.

Two men accused of producing or selling melamine-contaminated material for use in milk were sentenced to death and executed in 2009. Other defendants received prison terms ranging from several years to life.

Chinese authorities said the contamination often occurred before milk reached processing plants. Some middlemen watered down raw milk to increase volume, then added melamine so the milk would still pass basic protein tests. The scandal nevertheless raised questions about why dairy companies’ quality-control systems failed to detect the adulteration.

## Contaminated products reached foreign markets

The crisis quickly spread beyond mainland China because Chinese milk powder and milk-derived ingredients were used in processed foods exported around the world.

Sanlu formula and other Chinese dairy products had been exported or distributed to markets including parts of Asia and Africa. Governments in **Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Malaysia, the Philippines, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Vietnam, Burundi and Gabon**, among others, investigated products, issued bans or ordered recalls.

The list of affected goods expanded beyond formula to include:

- Milk powder  
- Chocolate and candy  
- Biscuits and cookies  
- Instant coffee and tea drinks  
- Ice cream and frozen desserts  
- Products containing Chinese-made milk protein or creamer  

One of the most widely recognized recalls involved **White Rabbit candy**, a well-known Chinese confection that was removed from shelves in several countries after tests detected melamine.

International agencies, including the World Health Organization, said the incident demonstrated the difficulty of tracing ingredients through a globalized food supply.

## FDA warned consumers and expanded testing

In the United States, the **Food and Drug Administration** said infant formula manufactured in China was not approved for legal import and was not believed to be part of the mainstream US formula supply.

However, the agency warned that Chinese-made formula could have entered the country through ethnic grocery stores, informal distribution networks or personal imports. The FDA advised consumers not to use infant formula manufactured in China and urged caregivers to seek medical attention if a child who had consumed such formula developed symptoms of kidney problems.

The agency also:

- Increased inspections of imported foods containing milk-derived ingredients  
- Tested products for melamine and related compounds  
- Issued import alerts allowing suspect products to be detained without physical examination  
- Worked with state authorities to remove Chinese-made formula found in some stores  
- Published updates and lists of affected or recalled products  

US recalls eventually included several imported foods containing Chinese dairy ingredients, although FDA officials said the country’s principal infant-formula supply was not affected.

The agency initially treated any detectable melamine in infant formula as unacceptable. It later established risk-based interim thresholds for some foods, while maintaining a stricter position for infant formula because babies could consume large quantities relative to their body weight.

## A crisis of confidence

The scandal became a major test of China’s food-safety system. It revealed fragmented regulation, weak testing, pressure to suppress bad news and financial incentives to cheat within a rapidly expanding dairy industry.

Beijing responded by ordering nationwide inspections, closing some producers and revising food-safety laws. Authorities also offered medical examinations and treatment for affected children, though some families said compensation was inadequate and efforts to seek independent legal redress were obstructed.

The consequences lasted long after contaminated products disappeared from shelves. Many Chinese parents turned to foreign brands, creating a booming market for imported formula and, in later years, contributing to shortages and purchasing restrictions in several countries.

For families whose children died or suffered lasting kidney damage, the scandal was more than a regulatory failure. It was a betrayal of trust in one of the most basic products parents buy for their children.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
